101.solution: Rewrite as a linear ODE: \(x(x-1)\frac{dy}{dx}-(x-2)y=x^{3}(2x-1)\), i.e. \(\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{x-2}{x(x-1)}y=\frac{x^{2}(2x-1)}{x-1}\). With partial fractions \(\frac{2-x}{x(x-1)}=\frac{-2}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1}\), the integrating factor is \(\text{I.F.}=e^{\int(-\frac{2}{x}+\frac{1}{x-1})dx}=e^{-2\log x+\log(x-1)}=\frac{x-1}{x^{2}}\). Then \(y\cdot\frac{x-1}{x^{2}}=\int\frac{x-1}{x^{2}}\cdot\frac{x^{2}(2x-1)}{x-1}\,dx=\int(2x-1)\,dx=x^{2}-x+c\). Multiplying through by \(\frac{x^{2}}{x-1}\): \(y(x-1)=x^{2}(x^{2}-x)+cx^{2}=x^{3}(x-1)+cx^{2}\).

102.subtopic: Line — Equation, Direction Cosines, and Vector Form
102.solution: The line of intersection of two planes is along \(\bar{n}_{1}\times\bar{n}_{2}\), where \(\bar{n}_{1}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2\hat{k}\) and \(\bar{n}_{2}=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}\). The cross product is \(\bar{n}_{1}\times\bar{n}_{2}=(-1-2)\hat{i}-(1-6)\hat{j}+(1+3)\hat{k}=-3\hat{i}+5\hat{j}+4\hat{k}\). Its magnitude is \(\sqrt{9+25+16}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}\). Hence the direction cosines are \(\frac{-3}{5\sqrt{2}},\frac{5}{5\sqrt{2}},\frac{4}{5\sqrt{2}}\).

103.solution: Let the parts be \(x\) and \(20-x\), and maximise \(z=x^{3}(20-x)^{2}\). Then \(\frac{dz}{dx}=3x^{2}(20-x)^{2}+x^{3}\cdot 2(20-x)(-1)=x^{2}(20-x)[3(20-x)-2x]=x^{2}(20-x)(60-5x)\). Setting \(\frac{dz}{dx}=0\) gives \(x=12\) (rejecting \(x=0,20\)). The second-derivative test confirms a maximum at \(x=12\), so the parts are \(12\) and \(8\).

104.subtopic: Equation of Line — Rotation, Angle, and Bisector
104.solution: Diagonal \(AC\) joins \(A(2,-1)\) and \(C(2,3)\): it is vertical (slope \(=\infty\)). Diagonal \(BD\) joins \(B(0,2)\) and \(D(4,0)\): slope \(m=\frac{0-2}{4-0}=-\frac{1}{2}\). The acute angle a vertical line makes with a line of slope \(m\) is \(\theta\) with \(\tan\theta=\left|\frac{1}{m}\right|=2\). Hence \(\theta=\tan^{-1}2\).

105.subtopic: Tangent, Normal, Approximation, and Curve from Geometric Condition
105.solution: The shortest distance from the curve \(x=y^{2}\) to the line \(x-y+1=0\) (slope \(1\)) occurs where the tangent to the curve is parallel to the line. Differentiating \(x=y^{2}\): \(\frac{dx}{dy}=2y\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2y}=1\Rightarrow y=\frac{1}{2}\), \(x=\frac{1}{4}\). The point is \(\left(\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}\right)\). Distance \(=\frac{\left|\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}+1\right|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}=\frac{3/4}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{8}\).

106.subtopic: Equation of Circle from Diameter, Centre, and Concentric Conditions
106.solution: Factor the pair of lines: \(x^{2}-y^{2}-2x+4y-3=(x-1)^{2}-(y-2)^{2}=(x+y-3)(x-y+1)=0\). The two diameters are \(x+y=3\) and \(x-y=-1\); their intersection (the centre) is \((1,2)\). Since the circle passes through \((1,1)\), the radius is \(\sqrt{(1-1)^{2}+(2-1)^{2}}=1\). Equation: \((x-1)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=1\).

108.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
108.solution: Normals are \((1,-2,3)\) and \((1,\alpha,2)\). With \(\cos\theta=\frac{1}{14}\): \(\frac{1-2\alpha+6}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{5+\alpha^{2}}}=\frac{1}{14}\), so \(14(7-2\alpha)=\sqrt{14}\sqrt{5+\alpha^{2}}\). Squaring: \(14(7-2\alpha)^{2}=5+\alpha^{2}\Rightarrow 55\alpha^{2}-392\alpha+681=0\). The difference between the two roots is \(\frac{\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{|a|}=\frac{\sqrt{392^{2}-4(55)(681)}}{55}=\frac{\sqrt{3844}}{55}=\frac{62}{55}\).

109.subtopic: Distance, Foot of Perpendicular, Projection, and Mirror Image
109.solution: Both lines have direction \(\bar{b}=(2,3,4)\), \(|\bar{b}|=\sqrt{29}\). With points \(\bar{a}_{1}=(k,4,3)\), \(\bar{a}_{2}=(2,4,7)\), \(\bar{a}_{2}-\bar{a}_{1}=(2-k,0,4)\). The shortest distance for parallel lines is \(\frac{|\bar{b}\times(\bar{a}_{2}-\bar{a}_{1})|}{|\bar{b}|}\). Compute \(\bar{b}\times(\bar{a}_{2}-\bar{a}_{1})=(12,\,-4k,\,3k-6)\), so \(\frac{\sqrt{144+16k^{2}+(3k-6)^{2}}}{\sqrt{29}}=\frac{13}{\sqrt{29}}\). Thus \(144+16k^{2}+(3k-6)^{2}=169\Rightarrow 25k^{2}-36k+11=0\Rightarrow k=1\) (or \(11/25\), and \(k=1\) is the listed value).

110.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
110.solution: The direction ratios are \((2,-4,1)\) and \((-1,2,3)\). \(\cos\theta=\left|\frac{(2)(-1)+(-4)(2)+(1)(3)}{\sqrt{4+16+1}\,\sqrt{1+4+9}}\right|=\left|\frac{-7}{\sqrt{21}\sqrt{14}}\right|=\frac{7}{7\sqrt{6}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\). Hence \(\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\right)\).

111.subtopic: Tangent, Normal, Approximation, and Curve from Geometric Condition
111.solution: For \(y^{2}=6x\): \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3}{y}\). For \(9x^{2}+by^{2}=16\): \(18x+2by\frac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{9x}{by}\). Orthogonality requires the product of slopes \(=-1\): \(\frac{3}{y}\cdot\left(-\frac{9x}{by}\right)=-1\Rightarrow\frac{27x}{by^{2}}=1\). Using \(y^{2}=6x\): \(\frac{27x}{b(6x)}=1\Rightarrow\frac{27}{6b}=1\Rightarrow b=\frac{9}{2}\).

112.subtopic: Trig Identities, Compound Angle, and Equations
112.solution: \(\sqrt{3}\cot20^{\circ}-4\cos20^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}\cos20^{\circ}-4\sin20^{\circ}\cos20^{\circ}}{\sin20^{\circ}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}\cos20^{\circ}-2\sin40^{\circ}}{\sin20^{\circ}}\). Writing \(\sqrt{3}\cos20^{\circ}=2\sin60^{\circ}\cos20^{\circ}=\sin80^{\circ}+\sin40^{\circ}\), the numerator becomes \(\sin80^{\circ}-\sin40^{\circ}=2\cos60^{\circ}\sin20^{\circ}=\sin20^{\circ}\). Hence the value is \(\frac{\sin20^{\circ}}{\sin20^{\circ}}=1\).

113.solution: With \(|\bar a|=1,|\bar b|=4,\bar a\cdot\bar b=2\): \(|\bar a\times\bar b|^{2}=|\bar a|^{2}|\bar b|^{2}-(\bar a\cdot\bar b)^{2}=16-4=12\). For \(\bar c=2(\bar a\times\bar b)-3\bar b\), since \(\bar b\cdot(\bar a\times\bar b)=0\), \(|\bar c|^{2}=4(12)+9(16)=192\). Also \(\bar b\cdot\bar c=2\bar b\cdot(\bar a\times\bar b)-3|\bar b|^{2}=-48\). Then \(\cos\theta=\frac{\bar b\cdot\bar c}{|\bar b||\bar c|}=\frac{-48}{4\cdot 8\sqrt{3}}=\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}\), giving \(\theta=\frac{5\pi}{6}\).

114.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
114.solution: \([\bar a\bar b\bar d]\bar c-[\bar a\bar b\bar c]\bar d=((\bar a\times\bar b)\cdot\bar d)\bar c-((\bar a\times\bar b)\cdot\bar c)\bar d=(\bar a\times\bar b)\times(\bar c\times\bar d)\). Its magnitude is \(|\bar a\times\bar b|\,|\bar c\times\bar d|\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\). With \(\bar a\cdot\bar b=\frac{1}{2}\Rightarrow\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) so \(|\bar a\times\bar b|=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\); likewise \(|\bar c\times\bar d|=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). Hence value \(=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{8}\).

115.solution: Here \(\bar a\cdot\bar b=(4)(1)+(3)(-2)+(1)(2)=0\), so \(\bar a\perp\bar b\). Using \(\bar a\times(\bar a\times\bar b)=(\bar a\cdot\bar b)\bar a-|\bar a|^{2}\bar b=-|\bar a|^{2}\bar b\). Applying \(\bar a\times(\bar a\times\cdot)\) twice multiplies by \(|\bar a|^{2}\) each pair: \(\bar a\times(\bar a\times(\bar a\times(\bar a\times\bar b)))=|\bar a|^{4}\bar b\). With \(|\bar a|^{2}=16+9+1=26\), \(|\bar a|^{4}=676\), so the result is \(676\,\bar b\).

116.subtopic: Binomial Distribution — Mean, Variance, and Parameter Estimation

117.solution: Given \(q\) is F, so \(p\wedge q\) is F. Since \((p\wedge q)\leftrightarrow r\) is T and \(p\wedge q\) is F, \(r\) must be F. Then \(p\wedge r\) is F (since \(r=\)F), so a conditional with a false antecedent, \((p\wedge r)\rightarrow(p\vee r)\), is always T. (\(p\wedge q\), \(p\vee r\), \(p\wedge r\) are not guaranteed true.)

118.subtopic: Negation, Equivalence, Tautology, and Switch Circuits
118.solution: \((\sim p\wedge q)\vee(\sim p\wedge\sim q)\vee(p\wedge\sim q)\equiv\sim p\wedge(q\vee\sim q)\vee(p\wedge\sim q)\equiv\sim p\vee(p\wedge\sim q)\equiv(\sim p\vee p)\wedge(\sim p\vee\sim q)\equiv\sim p\vee\sim q\).

119.subtopic: Probability Distribution — Constants, Expectation, and Variance

120.subtopic: Basic Probability — Events, Conditional, and Complement

121.subtopic: Area Bounded by Curves, Axes, and Lines
121.solution: In the first quadrant the ellipse \(\frac{x^{2}}{9}+\frac{y^{2}}{4}=1\) gives \(y=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{9-x^{2}}\). Quarter-ellipse area \(=\int_{0}^{3}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{9-x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{9}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{3\pi}{2}\). The line \(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{y}{2}=1\) and the axes form a triangle of area \(\frac{1}{2}(3)(2)=3\). Required area between ellipse arc and line \(=\frac{3\pi}{2}-3=\frac{3}{2}(\pi-2)\) sq. units.

122.subtopic: Continuity at a Point — Finding Parameters
122.solution: Continuity at \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\) requires the left and right limits to be equal: \(m\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}+1=\sin\frac{\pi}{2}+n=1+n\). Hence \(\frac{m\pi}{2}=n\), i.e. \(n=\frac{m\pi}{2}\).

123.subtopic: Symmetry, King's Property, and Absolute Value
123.solution: \(x^{2}-x-2=(x-2)(x+1)\) is negative on \((-1,2)\) and positive on \([-2,-1]\). So \(\int_{-2}^{2}|x^{2}-x-2|dx=\int_{-2}^{-1}(x^{2}-x-2)dx+\int_{-1}^{2}-(x^{2}-x-2)dx\). Evaluating, the first integral \(=\frac{11}{6}\) and the second \(=\frac{27}{6}\)... computing precisely gives a total of \(\frac{19}{3}\).

124.solution: \(\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{\tan x}-e^{x}}{\tan x-x}=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{x}(e^{\tan x-x}-1)}{\tan x-x}\). As \(x\to 0\), \(\tan x-x\to 0\) and \(\frac{e^{u}-1}{u}\to 1\) with \(u=\tan x-x\), while \(e^{x}\to 1\). Hence the limit is \(1\cdot 1=1\).

125.subtopic: Area Bounded by Curves, Axes, and Lines
125.solution: For \(x^{2}=20y\), \(4a=20\Rightarrow a=5\); vertex \((0,0)\), focus \((0,5)\). The latus rectum has length \(4a=20\) with endpoints \((-10,5)\) and \((10,5)\). The triangle formed with the vertex has base \(20\) and height \(5\): area \(=\frac{1}{2}\times 20\times 5=50\) sq. units.

126.subtopic: Symmetry, King's Property, and Absolute Value
126.solution: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{1+x+x^{2}}-\sqrt{1-x+x^{2}}\). Then \(f(-x)=\sqrt{1-x+x^{2}}-\sqrt{1+x+x^{2}}=-f(x)\), so \(f\) is odd. The integral of an odd function over the symmetric interval \([-1,1]\) is \(0\).

127.subtopic: Basic Probability — Events, Conditional, and Complement
127.solution: From \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) with replacement, total outcomes \(=16\). Count pairs with \(p^{2}\ge 4q\): for \(p=2\) (\(p^{2}=4\)): \(q=1\) (1 case); \(p=3\) (\(9\ge 4q\Rightarrow q\le 2.25\)): \(q=1,2\) (2 cases); \(p=4\) (\(16\ge 4q\Rightarrow q\le 4\)): \(q=1,2,3,4\) (4 cases); \(p=1\): none. Total favourable \(=7\). Probability \(=\frac{7}{16}\).

128.solution: For \(f(x)=\frac{2x+3}{3x+4}\): assuming \(f(x_{1})=f(x_{2})\) leads to \((2x_{1}+3)(3x_{2}+4)=(2x_{2}+3)(3x_{1}+4)\Rightarrow x_{1}=x_{2}\), so \(f\) is one-one. Solving \(y=\frac{2x+3}{3x+4}\) for \(x\) gives \(x=\frac{3-4y}{3y-2}\), valid for all \(y\) except \(y=\frac{2}{3}\). Hence \(f\) is one-one and onto for \(y\neq\frac{2}{3}\).

129.subtopic: Algebraic Equations, Locus, and Cube Roots
129.solution: Let \(z=x+iy\). \(|z+1-i|=|z-1+i|\) gives \((x+1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=(x-1)^{2}+(y+1)^{2}\). Expanding: \(4x-4y=0\Rightarrow x=y\), a straight line through the origin with slope \(1\), lying in the first and third quadrants.

130.solution: Partial fractions: \(\frac{2x+3}{(x-1)(x^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^{2}+1}\) gives \(A=\frac{5}{2},B=-\frac{5}{2},C=-\frac{1}{2}\). Integrating: \(\frac{5}{2}\log(x-1)-\frac{5}{4}\log(x^{2}+1)-\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x+A=\log\{(x-1)^{5/2}(x^{2}+1)^{-5/4}\}-\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}x+A\). Comparing the exponent of \((x^{2}+1)\) gives \(a=-\frac{5}{4}\).

131.solution: Continuous compounding (or the equivalent ratio model): \(400\) doubles to \(800\) in \(6\) years, so the growth factor per year is \(2^{1/6}\). After \(33\) years, amount \(=400\cdot 2^{33/6}=400\cdot 2^{5.5}=400\cdot 32\cdot\sqrt{2}=400\cdot 32\cdot 1.4142=18101.76\).

132.solution: If \(\bar a,\bar b\) are unit vectors and \(|\bar a+\bar b|=1\): \(|\bar a+\bar b|^{2}=1+1+2\bar a\cdot\bar b=1\Rightarrow\bar a\cdot\bar b=-\frac{1}{2}\). Thus \(\cos\theta=-\frac{1}{2}\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

133.solution: Total triangles from \(20\) vertices \(=\binom{20}{3}=1140\). Triangles using exactly two sides of the polygon (three consecutive vertices) \(=20\). Triangles using exactly one side \(=20\times 16=320\) (each side with a third vertex not adjacent). Triangles with no side \(=1140-20-320=800\).

134.subtopic: Trigonometric Integrals - Rational and Substitution Forms

135.subtopic: Trig Identities, Compound Angle, and Equations
135.solution: With \(A+B=\frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\cos B=\sin A\), so \(\cos A\cos B=\cos A\sin A=\frac{1}{2}\sin 2A\). The maximum of \(\sin 2A\) is \(1\), so the maximum value is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

136.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
136.solution: A vector orthogonal to \(\bar a=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k\) and coplanar with \(\bar b=\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k\), \(\bar c=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k\) is \(\bar a\times(\bar b\times\bar c)=(\bar a\cdot\bar c)\bar b-(\bar a\cdot\bar b)\bar c\). Here \(\bar a\cdot\bar c=4\), \(\bar a\cdot\bar b=4\), so \(=4\bar b-4\bar c=4(-\hat j+\hat k)\). Magnitude \(=4\sqrt{2}\).

137.subtopic: Angle, Distance, and Geometry of Pair

138.solution: For \(y_{1}=x^{x}\): \(\log y_{1}=x\log x\Rightarrow y_{1}'=x^{x}(1+\log x)\). For \(y_{2}=x^{1/x}\): \(\log y_{2}=\frac{\log x}{x}\Rightarrow y_{2}'=x^{1/x}\cdot\frac{1}{x^{2}}(1-\log x)\). Hence \(\frac{dy}{dx}=x^{x}(1+\log x)+x^{1/x}\frac{1}{x^{2}}(1-\log x)\).

140.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Identities, Equations, Principal Values, and Sums
140.solution: Let \(a=\frac{x}{2},b=\frac{y}{2},c=\frac{z}{2}\). When \(\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b+\tan^{-1}c=\frac{\pi}{2}\), the standard result gives \(ab+bc+ca=1\). Hence \(\frac{xy}{4}+\frac{yz}{4}+\frac{zx}{4}=1\Rightarrow xy+yz+zx=4\).

141.subtopic: Properties of Triangles — Sine/Cosine Rules and Projection
141.solution: Using the cosine rule \(\cos A=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2bc}\) etc., the given relation \(\frac{2\cos A}{a}+\frac{\cos B}{b}+\frac{2\cos C}{c}=\frac{a}{bc}+\frac{b}{ca}\) simplifies (multiplying through by \(2abc\)) to \(2(b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2})+(a^{2}+c^{2}-b^{2})+2(a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2})=2a^{2}+2b^{2}\), which reduces to \(a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}\). Thus the triangle is right-angled at \(A\): \(\angle A=\frac{\pi}{2}\).

143.solution: \(y=\log x^{3}+3\sin^{-1}x+kx^{2}=3\log x+3\sin^{-1}x+kx^{2}\). So \(y'=\frac{3}{x}+\frac{3}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}+2kx\). At \(x=\frac{1}{2}\): \(y'=6+\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}/2}+k=6+2\sqrt{3}+k\). Setting this equal to \(2\sqrt{3}\): \(6+2\sqrt{3}+k=2\sqrt{3}\Rightarrow k=-6\).

144.subtopic: Properties of Triangles — Sine/Cosine Rules and Projection
144.solution: If \(a,b,c\) are in A.P., \(a+c=2b\), so \(s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}=\frac{3b}{2}\). Using half-angle formulae, \(\tan\frac{A}{2}\tan\frac{C}{2}=\frac{s-b}{s}=\frac{\frac{3b}{2}-b}{\frac{3b}{2}}=\frac{b/2}{3b/2}=\frac{1}{3}\).

145.subtopic: Trig Identities, Compound Angle, and Equations

146.solution: The shaded region lies to the right, bounded above by the line \(x-y=0\) and below by the line \(x+y=0\). A test point inside the region, e.g. \((2,0)\), gives \(x-y=2\ge 0\) and \(x+y=2\ge 0\). Hence the solution set is \(x-y\ge 0,\;x+y\ge 0\).
146.note: Read stem figure (image16.png): shaded wedge to the right between x-y=0 (upper boundary) and x+y=0 (lower boundary). Test point (2,0) satisfies both inequalities of option A.

147.subtopic: Properties of Triangles — Sine/Cosine Rules and Projection
147.solution: Expand: \(a\cos(B-\theta)+b\cos(A+\theta)=\cos\theta(a\cos B+b\cos A)+\sin\theta(a\sin B-b\sin A)\). By the projection rule \(a\cos B+b\cos A=c\), and by the sine rule \(a\sin B-b\sin A=0\). Hence the expression equals \(c\cos\theta\).

148.solution: \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&\tan x\\-\tan x&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(|A|=1+\tan^{2}x=\sec^{2}x\), \(A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\sec^{2}x}\begin{bmatrix}1&-\tan x\\\tan x&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(A^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1&-\tan x\\\tan x&1\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(A^{T}A^{-1}=\frac{1}{1+\tan^{2}x}\begin{bmatrix}1-\tan^{2}x&-2\tan x\\2\tan x&1-\tan^{2}x\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos 2x&-\sin 2x\\\sin 2x&\cos 2x\end{bmatrix}\).

149.subtopic: Order, Degree, Formation of ODE, and Verification of Solutions
149.solution: Given \(\sqrt{\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}=\sqrt[5]{\frac{dy}{dx}-5}\). Raising both sides to the 10th power: \(\left(\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}\right)^{5}=\left(\frac{dy}{dx}-5\right)^{2}\). Order \(=2\) (highest derivative) and degree \(=5\) (its power). Order + degree \(=2+5=7\).

150.subtopic: Order, Degree, Formation of ODE, and Verification of Solutions
150.solution: Differentiate \(x^{2}y=4e^{x}+c\) w.r.t. \(x\): \(2xy+x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}=4e^{x}\). Since \(4e^{x}=x^{2}y-c\) is not eliminated directly, write the relation as \(x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}+2xy-4e^{x}=0\), the differential equation of the family.
